sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.summary: Introduces Chapter 2 on excavation stability, covering two fundamental excavation types: open cut (stable side slopes) and braced (laterally supported vertical/sloped sides). Lists chapter topics including trenching, deep excavation systems, rock excavation, and groundwater control. Identifies primary site conditions controlling excavation system selection: soil/rock type, stratigraphy, strength, consolidation parameters, and groundwater.
sections.body:
This chapter covers the methods of evaluating the stability of shallow and deep excavations. There are two basic types of excavations: 1) open cut excavations where stability is achieved by providing stable side slopes and 2) braced excavations where vertical or sloped sides are supported laterally by internal or external structural elements. The topics in this chapter include:
- Open cut excavations,
- Trenching,
- Deep excavation systems,
- Rock excavation, and
- Groundwater control.

The primary site conditions controlling the selection and design of an excavation system include soil and rock type and stratigraphy, soil and rock strength and consolidation parameters, and groundwater conditions. These can be identified using methods described in Chapters 2 and 3 of DM 7.1 and FHWA (2017). Additional considerations include the required excavation depth, side and bottom stability, construction procedures, excavation support system stability, and vertical and lateral movements of adjacent areas and existing structures.
key_points: Two basic excavation types: open cut (stable slopes) and braced (laterally supported sides).
Chapter covers open cut, trenching, deep excavation systems, rock excavation, and groundwater control.
Key site conditions: soil/rock type, stratigraphy, strength, consolidation parameters, and groundwater.
Additional design considerations include excavation depth, bottom/side stability, construction procedures, and effects on adjacent structures.
Site investigation methods referenced from DM 7.1 Chapters 2 and 3 and FHWA (2017).
sections.applicability: Applies as an introductory overview whenever evaluating or designing any type of excavation system (open cut or braced).

sections.title: OPEN CUT EXCAVATIONS
sections.summary: Container section covering open cut excavation design, including sloped excavations, vertical excavations in clay and rock, and other design considerations. Addresses slope stability evaluation methods, failure modes by soil/rock type, and improvement strategies. References DM 7.1 Chapter 7 for stability analysis methods.
key_points: Open cut excavations rely on stable side slopes rather than structural support elements.
Slope stability is influenced by soil/rock type, groundwater, time, and disturbance.
Stability improvement options include lowering the top of slope, reducing slope angle, and controlling surcharge loading.
sections.applicability: Applies when designing or evaluating open cut excavations in any soil or rock type without lateral structural support.

sections.title: Sloped Excavations
sections.summary: Covers evaluation of stability for sloped open cut excavations in soils and rocks using DM 7.1 Chapter 7 methods. Describes failure modes by material: side-slope failures in clays with increasing shear strength, base-extending failures in clays with constant shear strength, limited base instability in coarse-grained soils with seepage control, and joint/fault-controlled failures in rock. Warns of special considerations for problem soils and time-dependent stability reduction.
sections.body:
The methods described in Chapter 7 of DM 7.1 may be used to evaluate the stability of sloped excavations in soils and rocks. In clay soils, instability typically involves side slopes but may also include soils below the base of the excavation. Clay soils that increase in shear strength with depth typically exhibit failures that occur on the side slopes. For clay soils that exhibit relatively constant shear strength with depth, the failure may extend into the base of the excavation. In coarse-grained soils, instability usually does not extend significantly below the base of the excavation, provided seepage is controlled. In rock, stability is often controlled by adversely orientated planes of weaknesses such as joints, foliation planes, or faults.

In some problem soils, and in rocks with adversely orientated geologic planes of weaknesses, special considerations are needed when evaluating stability of open cut excavations as discussed in Section 2-7. In any soil, the stability of excavated slopes may decrease with time, saturation, and disturbance. Some soils may not conform to common shear strength correlations used in design. For example, the properties of residual soil, which cover about half of Earth's land mass, are difficult to relate to stress history. Local knowledge may be helpful when determining the analysis approach in these problem soils.

Slope stability can be improved by reducing the driving forces that cause instability. The top of a slope can be lowered, or the slope angle can be reduced, if an adequate factor of safety against instability is not achieved. Surcharge loading from equipment and/or stockpiles should be kept away from the top of an excavation when these negatively impact stability.
key_points: Use DM 7.1 Chapter 7 methods for slope stability evaluation in soils and rock.
Clays with increasing shear strength with depth: failures typically on side slopes only.
Clays with constant shear strength: failure may extend into excavation base.
Coarse-grained soils: instability rarely extends below base if seepage is controlled.
Rock stability governed by adversely oriented joints, foliation planes, or faults.
Slope stability decreases with time, saturation, and disturbance; residual soils require local knowledge.
Mitigation: lower top of slope, reduce slope angle, keep surcharges away from excavation crest.
sections.applicability: Applies when evaluating or designing sloped (non-vertical) open cut excavations in any soil or rock type.

sections.title: Vertical Excavations
sections.summary: Container section addressing vertical open cut excavations, covering critical depth calculations for clay soils and stability considerations for rock excavations. Includes the governing equation for maximum vertical cut depth in clay and references OSHA requirements for excavations deeper than 5 ft.
key_points: Vertical cuts in clay have a calculable critical depth (Hcrit) beyond which failure will occur.
Rock excavations may stand vertically depending on rock quality and absence of adversely oriented discontinuities.
OSHA requires sloping or support for all excavations greater than 5 ft in depth.
sections.applicability: Applies when considering unsupported vertical cuts in clay or rock materials.

sections.title: Clay Soils
sections.summary: Defines the critical depth (Hcrit) of an unsupported vertical cut in clay as a function of undrained shear strength and total unit weight (Eq. 2-1). Notes that progressive deterioration occurs due to shear strength changes over time and stress release from excavation. Cites OSHA requirement to slope or support all excavations greater than 5 ft deep.
sections.body:
Many cuts in clays will stand with vertical slopes for a period of time before failure occurs. The maximum depth of a vertical cut in clay, or critical depth, (Hcrit) is defined as:

Hcrit = 4 * su / γt  (2-1)

where:
su = undrained shear strength and
γt = total or moist unit weight of the clay.

However, changes in the shear strength of the clay with time and stress release resulting from the excavation can lead to progressive deterioration in stability. The Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) requires all excavations be sloped and trenches supported if greater than 5 ft in depth (OSHA 2020).
key_points: Critical depth Hcrit = 4su/γt defines the maximum stable height for an unsupported vertical cut in clay.
Clay cuts can stand temporarily but progressive shear strength reduction and stress release cause time-dependent failure.
OSHA (2020) mandates sloping or support for all excavations > 5 ft deep regardless of calculated critical depth.
Two parameters govern: undrained shear strength (su) and total/moist unit weight (γt).

equations.description: Critical depth of a vertical cut in clay: Hcrit = 4su / γt, where su is undrained shear strength and γt is total or moist unit weight of clay.

sections.applicability: Applies when assessing the maximum unsupported vertical cut depth in cohesive (clay) soils.

sections.title: Rock
sections.summary: Addresses vertical unsupported cuts in rock, noting that stability depends on rock quality, absence of adversely oriented joints and faults, and mobilized shear strength along structural features. References DM 7.1 Chapter 7 for rock slope stability analysis. Does not provide a closed-form equation; stability is assessed on a case-by-case basis.
sections.body: Excavations in rock can be made vertical without support (rock bolts or tieback anchors) depending on the rock quality, lack of adversely oriented joints and faults, and sufficient mobilized shear strength along structural features to provide a stable condition. The stability of rock slopes is also covered in Chapter 7 of DM 7.1.
key_points: Rock can stand vertically without support when rock quality is high and adversely oriented discontinuities are absent.
Rock bolts or tieback anchors provide support where rock quality or discontinuity orientation is unfavorable.
Stability depends on mobilized shear strength along joints, faults, and other structural features.
DM 7.1 Chapter 7 provides the analysis framework for rock slope stability.
sections.applicability: Applies when evaluating unsupported vertical cuts in rock formations.

sections.title: Other Design Considerations for Open Cut Excavations
sections.summary: Covers ancillary design considerations for open cut excavations beyond slope stability, focusing on dewatering requirements and groundwater control. Notes that dewatering increases effective stress and can cause settlement in adjacent structures. Introduces the use of low-permeability cutoff trenches (soil-bentonite or soil-cement-bentonite) to manage groundwater between the excavation and nearby structures.
sections.body: Dewatering may be required to allow construction without water in the excavation (sometimes referred to as 'in the dry'). Dewatering increases effective stress and can cause settlement under nearby structures. It may be necessary to consider installation of a low permeability cutoff trench, filled with soil-bentonite or soil-cement-bentonite mixtures, between the excavation and adjacent structures to control groundwater-related settlement.
key_points: Dewatering ('in the dry') may be required for open cut construction in groundwater-bearing soils.
Dewatering raises effective stress in surrounding soils, potentially causing settlement under adjacent structures.
Low-permeability cutoff trenches (soil-bentonite or soil-cement-bentonite) can be installed to limit groundwater drawdown effects on nearby structures.
sections.applicability: Applies when open cut excavations are planned in areas with shallow groundwater or adjacent to existing structures sensitive to settlement.

sections.title: TRENCHING
sections.summary: Top-level container section covering all aspects of trenching, including site exploration, trench stability factors, and the various support systems regulated by OSHA. Addresses how subsurface conditions, groundwater, surface loads, and vibrations affect trench design and worker safety.
key_points: Trenching projects require site exploration programs to define soil and groundwater conditions over the full project extent.
OSHA (2020) regulates excavation support for trenches; principal stability factors include lateral earth pressures, bottom heave, and groundwater infiltration.
Support systems covered include trench shields, hydraulic shoring, timber shoring, and steel shoring.
Shoring and sheeting plans must be certified by a registered PE; trenches >20 ft deep require a licensed PE approval.
sections.applicability: Applies whenever trenching operations are planned, designed, or constructed on DoD projects.

sections.title: Site Exploration
sections.summary: Describes exploration program requirements for trenching projects, which frequently extend over long distances. Emphasizes the need to characterize soil and groundwater conditions along the full project extent so the shoring system design can be adjusted for varying subsurface conditions.
sections.body: Individual trenching projects frequently extend over long distances. An exploration program should be performed to define the soil and groundwater conditions over the full extent of the project so that the design of the shoring system can be adjusted to accommodate varying subsurface conditions.
key_points: Trenching projects often span long distances, requiring comprehensive exploration programs.
Exploration must cover the full project extent to capture varying subsurface conditions.
Results are used to adjust shoring system design along the project alignment.
sections.applicability: Applies during the planning and design phase of any trenching project to determine shoring requirements along the alignment.

sections.title: Trench Stability
sections.summary: Identifies principal and external factors influencing trench stability per OSHA (2020). Principal factors are lateral earth pressures on wall support, bottom heave, and infiltrating groundwater pressure/erosion. External factors include surface surcharge, vibration, groundwater seepage, and surface water flow.
sections.body:
Excavation support for trenches is regulated by OSHA (2020). Principal factors influencing trench stability are the lateral earth pressures (see Chapter 4) on the wall support system, bottom heave, and the pressure and erosive effects of infiltrating groundwater (see Chapter 6 of DM 7.1). Additional external factors which influence trench stability include:
- Surface surcharge loads,
- Vibration loads,
- Groundwater seepage, and
- Surface water flow.
key_points: OSHA (2020) governs trench excavation support requirements.
Principal stability factors: lateral earth pressures, bottom heave, and groundwater infiltration pressure/erosion.
External stability factors: surface surcharge, vibrations, groundwater seepage, and surface water flow.
Lateral earth pressure guidance is in Chapter 4; groundwater/seepage guidance is in DM 7.1 Chapter 6.
sections.applicability: Applies when evaluating the stability of any trench excavation where external loads or groundwater conditions may affect the support system.

sections.title: Surface Surcharge Loads
sections.summary: Addresses the effect of surface loads adjacent to a trench on the support system. Loads between the excavation edge and the failure plane intersection with the ground surface must be considered. Directs the reader to Section 4-4.2 for earth pressure guidance from surface loading.
sections.body: Surface loads may be present adjacent to a trench and cause loading on the trench support system. The effects of surface loads should be considered if the load is between the edge of the excavation and the intersection of the ground surface with the possible failure plane. Section 4-4.2 provides additional guidance on earth pressures caused by surface loading.
key_points: Surface surcharge loads adjacent to a trench must be assessed for their effect on the support system.
Loads are relevant if located between the trench edge and the failure plane's ground surface intersection.
See Section 4-4.2 for detailed earth pressure methodology due to surface loading.
sections.applicability: Applies when surface loads (equipment, stockpiles, structures) exist adjacent to an open trench excavation.

sections.title: Vibration Loads
sections.summary: Covers the effects of vibrating machinery, blasting, dynamic loads, and earthquakes on trench stability. Notes that vibration effects are cumulative, especially dangerous in soft clays and loose contractive sands/silts, which can flow after disturbance. Blasting charge size should be minimized in trenches.
sections.body: The effects of vibrating machinery, blasting, other dynamic loads, and earthquakes in the vicinity of the excavation must be considered. The effects of vibrations are cumulative over periods of time and can be particularly dangerous in soft clays which amplify vibrations. In addition, vibrations from earthquakes or blasting can cause loose contractive sands and silts to fail as brittle materials at low strains. Once disturbed, these materials flow, which can result in catastrophic damage. Excavations in these types of soil are very problematic. While dense coarse-grained soils are also brittle and fail at low strains, they do not flow and are not problematic for excavations. If blasting is required in a trench, the size of the charge should be as small as possible, and the effect of vibrations on settlement of or damage to adjacent structures must be considered.
key_points: Vibration effects from machinery, blasting, and earthquakes are cumulative and must be evaluated.
Soft clays amplify vibrations; loose contractive sands and silts can flow catastrophically once disturbed at low strains.
Dense coarse-grained soils are brittle but do not flow — less problematic than loose sands/silts.
When blasting is necessary near a trench, minimize charge size and monitor effects on adjacent structures.
sections.applicability: Applies to trench excavations near vibration sources such as heavy equipment, blasting operations, or seismically active areas.

sections.title: Groundwater Seepage
sections.summary: Explains two groundwater-related failure modes in trenches: bottom heave (quick condition) caused by upward seepage gradient exceeding critical gradient, and internal erosion of fine sands and silts. Both result from inadequate dewatering. Design guidance for internal erosion is referenced to DM 7.1 Chapter 6.
sections.body:
Groundwater seepage at the bottom of an excavation can result in bottom heave. Bottom heave refers to upward movement of the base of the excavation caused by a high upward gradient that exceeds the critical gradient of the soil. This is also referred to as a quick condition. Heaving or quick soils lose all or most of their shear strength because the effective stress approaches zero. Bottom heave can occur in coarse-grained soils that are improperly dewatered.

In addition to heave, seepage can result in internal erosion, which is the movement of soil particles from within the soil structure. Fine sands and silts are most susceptible to internal erosion. Prediction methods and design for internal erosion are discussed in Chapter 6 of DM 7.1.
key_points: Bottom heave (quick condition) occurs when upward seepage gradient exceeds the critical gradient, reducing effective stress to near zero.
Bottom heave can affect coarse-grained soils when dewatering is inadequate.
Internal erosion — particle movement within the soil structure — is most likely in fine sands and silts.
See DM 7.1 Chapter 6 for internal erosion prediction methods and design guidance.
sections.applicability: Applies to trench excavations in high groundwater environments, particularly in fine-grained or poorly dewatered coarse-grained soils.

sections.title: Surface Water Flow
sections.summary: Addresses uncontrolled surface water intrusion into retained soil behind trench walls, which increases water content, may cause saturation, raises loads on the support system, and can reduce soil shear strength. Site drainage must divert surface water away from trenches, especially in the zone between the excavation edge and failure plane.
sections.body: Uncontrolled surface water can enter the retained soil, increase the water content, and potentially result in saturation. Saturation greatly increases loads on the wall support system and may reduce the shear strength of the soil. Site drainage should be designed to divert surface water away from trenches. This is especially important for the zone between the edge of the excavation and the intersection of a possible failure plane with the ground surface.
key_points: Surface water infiltration into retained soil can saturate it, increasing wall support loads and reducing shear strength.
Site drainage must be designed to divert surface water away from the trench.
The critical zone is between the trench edge and the failure plane's ground surface intersection.
sections.applicability: Applies to all trench excavations where surface runoff or precipitation could enter the retained soil zone adjacent to the trench.

sections.title: Support Systems
sections.summary: Introduces OSHA (2020) requirements for protective measures in trenches >5 ft deep (or shallower if cave-in risk exists). Describes the role of a 'competent person,' PE certification requirements, and the suite of support systems covered: trench shields, hydraulic shoring, timber shoring, and steel shoring. Cross braces must be horizontal, vertically spaced, and secured.
sections.body:
OSHA (2020) requires protective measures for any trench greater than 5 feet deep, except in stable rock. Protective measures are also required for some excavations at any point less than 5 feet deep where there is evidence of a potential cave-in as determined by a competent person. OSHA (2020) describes a competent person as someone capable of identifying hazards or unsafe working conditions who possesses authority to take corrective measures.

Shoring and sheeting plans should be certified by a registered professional engineer. For trenches greater than 20 feet deep, a licensed professional engineer must approve the design (OSHA 2020).

The commonly used excavation support systems discussed in the following sections include trench shields, hydraulic shoring, timber shoring, and steel shoring. Cross braces or trench jacks shall be placed in true horizontal position; spaced vertically; and secured to prevent sliding, falling, or kickouts.
key_points: OSHA requires protective measures for all trenches >5 ft deep, and shallower if cave-in potential exists.
A 'competent person' must identify hazards and has authority to implement corrective measures.
Shoring/sheeting plans require PE certification; trenches >20 ft deep require licensed PE design approval.
Cross braces and trench jacks must be truly horizontal, vertically spaced, and secured against sliding or kickout.
Primary support systems: trench shields, hydraulic shoring, timber shoring, and steel shoring.
sections.applicability: Applies to the selection and regulatory compliance of support systems for any trench excavation on DoD projects.

sections.title: OSHA Soil Types
sections.summary: Summarizes the three OSHA soil types (A, B, C) used for trench design, including their cohesive/granular descriptions, unconfined compressive strength ranges, approximate USCS classifications, and key exclusions/inclusions. Notes that OSHA definitions do not conform to USCS (ASTM D2487).
sections.body: OSHA (2020) defines Soil Types A, B, and C for the design of trenches as summarized in Table 2-1. Appendix A of the OSHA manual provides definitions of terms used in defining these soil types. OSHA's definitions do not conform to the Unified Soil Classification System (ASTM D2487).
key_points: OSHA classifies soils as Type A (strongest), B, or C (weakest) for trench design purposes.
Type A: cohesive soils with unconfined compressive strength >1.5 tsf; excludes fissured, previously disturbed, or vibration-affected soils.
Type B: cohesive soils 0.5–1.5 tsf and granular cohesionless soils; includes downgraded Type A soils.
Type C: cohesive soils <0.5 tsf and granular cohesionless soils; includes soils with layers dipping into excavation >4H:1V.
OSHA soil type definitions differ from USCS (ASTM D2487) classifications.
sections.applicability: Applies when classifying on-site soils for OSHA-compliant trench shoring and support system design.

sections.title: Trench Shield
sections.summary: Describes the trench shield — a prefabricated rigid steel support system placed within a vertical-walled excavation. Covers its use in most soils (except very dense/hard), OSHA depth limits (up to 20 ft for manufactured shields), allowance for up to 2 ft of excavation below the shield, and geometry requirements for sloped excavations.
sections.body:
A trench shield is a rigid prefabricated steel support system used in lieu of other types of shoring, which extends from the bottom of the excavation to the ground surface. The trench shield is placed within a wider excavation with vertical walls and protects the enclosed space from trench collapse. Piping systems or other structures are constructed within the shield, which is pulled ahead, as trenching and construction proceed. Figure 2-1(a) illustrates a trench shield. This system is useful in most soils with the exception of very dense or hard soils. The trench shield must extend to the ground surface of vertical excavations. Where part of the excavation is sloped, the trench shield extends 18 inches above the toe of the slope as shown in Figure 2-1(b). The trench shield must be designed for the full height of the excavation including the sloped portion above the trench shield.

Excavation depths of up to 20 feet are permitted by OSHA (2020) using manufactured trench shields designed in accordance with OSHA standards. These shields should be used in accordance with the manufacturer's specifications, recommendations, tabulated data, and limitations. Shield systems must not be subjected to loads exceeding those which the system was designed to withstand.

Excavations up to 2 feet below the shield are permitted when the shield is designed to resist the forces for the full depth of the trench. This type of excavation is only permitted when there is no indication of loss of soil from behind or below the bottom of the shield. When designing for an excavation below the bottom of the shield, consideration must be given to the potential for internal erosion or heaving. During use, the excavation should be observed for evidence of these problem conditions. Surcharge loading, vibrations, or loads from adjacent structures also must be considered.
key_points: Trench shields are prefabricated rigid steel systems pulled forward as construction progresses; useful in most soils except very dense or hard materials.
OSHA permits manufactured trench shields to 20 ft depth; must be used per manufacturer's specifications and not overloaded.
Shield must reach ground surface in vertical excavations; in sloped excavations, it must extend 18 in above the slope toe.
Up to 2 ft of excavation below the shield is permitted only if the shield is designed for full trench depth and no soil loss is occurring.
Internal erosion, heave, surcharge, and adjacent structure loads must all be evaluated when excavating below the shield bottom.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting trench shields as the protective system for trench excavations up to 20 ft deep in most soil types.

sections.title: Hydraulic Shoring
sections.summary: Describes hydraulic shoring consisting of aluminum hydraulic cylinder braces and heavy plywood (Finform) sheets. Covers its advantages over timber shoring (lower cost, no trench entry required), typical depth/width limits (~25 ft deep, up to 12 ft wide), and OSHA design tables for soil types A–C with and without wales.
sections.body:
Hydraulic shoring consists of aluminum hydraulic cylinder braces and heavy plywood (Finform) sheets. It has gained popularity over timber shoring, because it is less costly and does not require workers to enter a trench to construct the shoring. Table 2-2 and Table 2-3 provide hydraulic shoring requirements from OSHA (2020). Figure 2-2 illustrates typical applications of hydraulic shoring (OSHA 2020).

Hydraulic shoring can typically be used to a depth of about 25 feet with trench widths up to 12 feet. The trench width can be increased with cylinder extensions referred to as steel tube oversleeves. Hydraulic shoring design guidelines are found in OSHA (2020) Appendix D, Item (g).
key_points: Hydraulic shoring uses aluminum cylinder braces and heavy plywood (Finform); preferred over timber because workers need not enter the trench.
Applicable to depths up to ~25 ft and widths up to 12 ft; width can be extended using steel tube oversleeves.
OSHA Tables D-1.1 through D-1.4 govern cylinder spacing, diameter, and waler requirements for soil types A–C.
Trenches >20 ft deep require manufacturer's tabulated data and CFR Part 1926 Subpart P compliance.
2-inch diameter cylinders at widths 8–12 ft require structural steel tube oversleeves (3.5×3.5×0.1875 in).
sections.applicability: Applies when designing or selecting hydraulic shoring for trench excavations in OSHA soil types A, B, or C up to approximately 25 ft deep.

sections.title: Timber Shoring
sections.summary: Covers four timber shoring types (skeleton, close/tight, box, telescopic) and their applicability by soil and depth conditions. Addresses OSHA minimum requirements from Table 2-4, timber quality requirements, allowable compressive stress limits, slenderness ratio limit of 50, and conditions requiring licensed PE approval including depths >20 ft and submerged conditions.
sections.body:
Timber shoring uses a temporary structure made of wood to support a trench. The four types of timber shoring are illustrated in Figure 2-3. The systems use vertical uprights or horizontal timbers against the soil, which are supported by a system of wales and cross-braces. Skeleton shoring does not use continuous upright members and is applicable when running soils are not expected. It can be used to depths up to 20 feet. Close (tight) shoring uses continuous upright timbers to support the soil and is useful where seepage and cave-ins are expected. Box shoring uses horizontal timbers to support the soil. Box shoring is applicable to trenching in any soil and is only limited in depth by the structural strength and size of the timber. Telescopic shoring is used for very deep trenches and consists of nested trenches that decrease in width as the trench depth increases.

Timbers used for shoring must be sound and free from large or loose knots. Timber shoring must be designed and installed to the bottom of the excavation. Braces and uprights for timber shoring must be installed at the same time as the excavation. Braces and diagonal shores of timber should not be subjected to compressive stresses in excess of the allowable compressive stress. The allowable compressive stress will vary by species of wood. Additional information on the structural properties of timber can be found in Section 6-7.1.1.3 as well as the Wood Handbook (USDA 2010). The allowable compressive stress will decrease as the slenderness of the shoring member increases. The ratio of length to least width is typically limited to 50 or less.

Table 2-4 summarizes the OSHA (2020) minimum requirements for trench shoring. The data in the table are for nominal size timber with spacing measured center to center. A maximum of two feet of soil surcharge adjacent to the trench and a maximum equipment surcharge of 20,000 lb are assumed in the design. The region adjacent to the trench is defined as a horizontal distance on each side of the trench equal to its depth. OSHA (2020) indicates that tight sheeting, such as tongue and groove timber at least three inches thick or steel sheet piling, must be used when submerged conditions are encountered to resist the lateral water pressure and to reduce loss of fines behind the sheeting. Table 2-4 does not cover the case of submerged conditions. A licensed professional engineer must approve the design for trenches greater than 20 ft deep, submerged conditions, and other conditions as noted in Table 2-4.
key_points: Four timber shoring types: skeleton (no running soils, ≤20 ft), close/tight (seepage and cave-in risk), box (any soil, depth limited by timber size), and telescopic (very deep trenches).
All timbers must be sound; braces and uprights must be installed concurrently with excavation.
Allowable compressive stress varies by wood species; slenderness ratio (length/least width) must not exceed 50.
Table 2-4 OSHA minimums assume 2 ft soil surcharge and 20,000 lb equipment surcharge; horizontal stress: σ'h = (25H)+72 psf (Type A), (45H)+72 psf (Type B), (80H)+72 psf (Type C).
Timber specified as Douglas fir or equivalent with bending strength ≥ 1,500 psi; manufactured equivalents may substitute.
Tight sheeting (tongue and groove ≥3 in thick or steel sheet piling) required for submerged conditions.
Licensed PE approval required for trenches >20 ft, submerged conditions, and certain depth/soil/spacing combinations in Table 2-4.
sections.applicability: Applies when designing or selecting timber shoring for trench excavations in OSHA soil types A, B, or C, including evaluation of member sizing, surcharge assumptions, and submerged conditions.

sections.title: Deep Excavation Systems
sections.summary: Introduces the topic of deep excavation support systems, covering factors that influence wall design and selection, basal heave, movement prediction of walls and adjacent soil/structures, and construction. References FHWA (2008) and Clough and O'Rourke (1990) for further detail, and directs the reader to Chapter 4 for earth pressure discussion.
sections.body: The discussion of deep excavation support systems includes consideration of the factors that influence wall design and selection, design against basal heave, prediction of the movement of walls and the adjacent soil and structures, and construction. Further information can be found in FHWA (2008) and Clough and O'Rourke (1990). Detailed discussion of earth pressures is included in Chapter 4.
key_points: Deep excavation support systems are required for below-ground construction and must account for wall movement during construction.
Movement impacts on surrounding structures and the project built within the excavation must be evaluated.
Key references: FHWA (2008) and Clough and O'Rourke (1990); earth pressures detailed in Chapter 4.
sections.applicability: Applies when designing or selecting deep excavation support systems for below-ground construction projects.

sections.title: Types of Wall and Support Systems
sections.summary: Describes the major types of deep excavation wall systems (sheet piling, combined sheet piling, soldier piles and lagging, secant/tangent pile walls, deep soil mixing, concrete diaphragms) and support systems (rakers, cross-lot struts, tiebacks, soil nails, berms). Covers movement mechanisms, wall and support selection factors summarized in Tables 2-5 and 2-6, and movement profiles from Clough and O'Rourke (1990).
key_points: Wall movements depend on soil type/strength, groundwater, excavation depth/shape, wall/support stiffness, construction method, surcharge loads, and duration of support.
Three movement stages: (1) cantilever (unsupported wall, largest movement at top), (2) deep inward movement (basal), and (3) cumulative movement.

In sands and stiff-to-hard clays, cantilever movement dominates with triangular settlement distribution; in soft-to-medium clays, deep inward movement dominates with trapezoidal settlement distribution.
Major wall types: steel sheet piling, combined sheet piling, soldier piles (H-piles) and lagging, secant pile walls, tangent pile walls, deep soil mixing, and concrete diaphragms.
Support systems include internal (rakers, cross-lot struts/braces) and external (prestressed tieback anchors, soil nails) systems; berms supplement toe resistance.
Stiff/dense berms develop passive resistance with less movement than loose berms; low FOS against basal heave reduces berm effectiveness.
Selection factors for wall types summarized in Table 2-5; project conditions influencing support system selection summarized in Table 2-6.
figures: Figure 2-4 — Typical Profiles of Movement for Braced and Tieback Anchor Walls (after Clough and O'Rourke 1990)
Figure 2-5 — Examples of Combined Sheet Piling Cross Sections (after DeepEX Combined Sheet Pile Walls Software 2021)
Figure 2-6 — Examples of Support Systems (after USACE 1983b and FHWA 2015)
tables: Table 2-5 — Types of Walls and Factors Involved with Selection
Table 2-6 — Project Conditions that Influence the Selection of a Support System
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting and designing deep excavation wall and support systems for below-ground construction, particularly where adjacent structure protection and movement control are required.

sections.title: Site Considerations for Deep Excavations
sections.summary: Container section covering site-specific considerations that govern the selection and design of deep excavation support systems. Content is fully elaborated in subsections 2-4.2.1 (soil type influence) and 2-4.2.2 (groundwater influence), which address earth pressure conditions, wall selection, dewatering, and stability factors.
key_points: Site conditions — primarily soil type and groundwater — are the primary drivers for selecting deep excavation wall and support systems.
Detailed guidance on soil type and groundwater influences is provided in subsections 2-4.2.1 and 2-4.2.2 respectively.
sections.applicability: Applies whenever site conditions must be evaluated to select and design a deep excavation support system.

sections.title: Influence of Soil Type
sections.summary: Explains how soil type governs the choice of deep excavation wall and support system, referencing Table 2-7 as a selection guide. Covers how wall movement relative to soil determines at-rest, active, and passive earth pressure conditions; notes that active pressure mobilizes at much less movement than passive, and that restricting passive-side movement reduces mobilized resistance. Factors such as wall/support stiffness and excavation depth also affect actual pressures.
sections.body:
The type of soil supported by a deep excavation will influence the selection of an appropriate type of wall and support system. Table 2-7 provides a guide for this selection process based on soil type.

The soil type will also control the earth pressures and forces on deep excavation systems, which are discussed in detail in Chapter 4. Earth pressures depend on wall movement relative to the soil. When little to no movement occurs, the earth pressure condition is referred to as at-rest. The stress state in the soil approaches an active condition at locations where the wall moves away from the soil. This occurs behind the wall system above the base of the excavation. The stress state in the soil approaches a passive condition at locations where the wall moves toward the soil. This occurs on an embedded portion of the wall system below the base of the excavation. Different amounts of wall movement must occur to fully mobilize active and passive pressures. The movement required to mobilize active pressure is much lower than that required for passive pressure. Restricting wall movement in the passive case greatly reduces the mobilized passive earth pressure, but this is necessary in most design cases due to movement limitations.

Actual earth pressures depend on wall deformation, and this in turn depends on several factors including stiffness of wall and support system, stability of the base of the excavation, and depth of excavation. These factors are discussed in more detail in Sections 2-4.3 and 2-4.4.
key_points: Soil type governs both the wall/support system selection (Table 2-7) and the earth pressures imposed on the excavation system.

At-rest pressure applies when little to no wall movement occurs; active pressure develops as the wall moves away from the soil (above excavation base); passive pressure develops as the wall moves into the soil (embedded portion below excavation base).
Active pressure is fully mobilized at much smaller wall movements than passive pressure.
Restricting wall movement on the passive side significantly reduces mobilized passive resistance, which must be accounted for in design.
Actual earth pressures depend on wall deformation, which is controlled by wall and support stiffness, base stability, and excavation depth — covered further in Sections 2-4.3 and 2-4.4.
For soft to medium clays, high wall stiffness (e.g., concrete diaphragm) is preferred to reduce movements and basal heave; tieback anchors and soil nails may be unsuitable.
Sheet piling is difficult to drive and interlocks may separate in dense sands, gravels, and clayey sands; soils with boulders/residual floaters may require chisels, hydromills, or rock coring.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting a deep excavation wall and support system type based on subsurface soil conditions and evaluating resulting earth pressure regimes.

sections.title: Influence of Groundwater
sections.summary: Addresses how groundwater conditions must be evaluated during selection and design of deep excavations. Covers water pressure on impervious walls, risks of excess pore pressure (heave, loss of passive resistance, seepage, internal erosion, particle erosion), and the option of dewatering adjacent soil to improve stability and reduce wall loads, with the caution that dewatering can cause settlement.
sections.body:
Groundwater conditions must be evaluated during the selection and design of a deep excavation. Some walls are impervious and prevent seepage through the wall. Where water is retained, water pressures on the wall may be greater than earth pressure. Excess pore pressures at the base of an excavation can result in heave, loss of passive resistance, seepage, and internal erosion. Particle erosion can also occur between open pile interlocks, lagging, and gaps in tangent pile walls.

In some cases, the soil adjacent to and below an excavation can be dewatered to improve stability and reduce wall loads. Some walls are not watertight and will allow water to seep into the excavation. The adjacent water level will drop provided the water is removed from the excavation. Dewatering will tend to cause settlement that may be [continued on next page].
key_points: Groundwater conditions must be evaluated during both selection and design of deep excavation systems.
Impervious walls (e.g., concrete diaphragm, sheet pile) retain water, potentially causing wall water pressures that exceed earth pressures.
Excess pore pressures at the excavation base can cause heave, loss of passive resistance, seepage, and internal erosion.
Particle erosion is a risk at open pile interlocks, lagging gaps, and tangent pile wall gaps.
Dewatering adjacent soil can improve stability and reduce wall loads, but carries a risk of causing ground settlement in surrounding areas.
Non-watertight walls allow seepage into the excavation; the adjacent groundwater level drops if water is continuously removed.
sections.applicability: Applies when evaluating groundwater impacts on deep excavation wall selection, water pressure design, seepage control, and dewatering decisions.

sections.title: Wall and Excavation Stability
sections.summary: Introduces the key stability considerations for deep excavation wall systems, including structural design for earth and water pressure forces, thermal effects on internal bracing, frost penetration on tiebacks and struts, wall settlement, global stability, and basal heave. References Chapter 4 for force determination methods.
sections.body: The deep excavation wall and supports must be designed to carry the forces from the earth and water pressures. Chapter 4 provides detail on the methods used to determine these forces so that the structural design of the wall can be completed. Those designs should also include the effects of thermal expansion and contraction on internal bracing, as well as the effects of frost penetration on tiebacks and struts. In addition, wall settlement, global stability, and basal heave must be considered.
key_points: Walls and supports must be designed for earth and water pressure forces; see Chapter 4 for force determination methods.
Structural design must account for thermal expansion/contraction effects on internal bracing.
Frost penetration effects on tiebacks and struts must be included in design.
Wall settlement, global stability, and basal heave are all required design considerations for deep excavations.
sections.applicability: Applies to all deep excavation wall and support system designs where earth/water pressures, thermal effects, and stability must be evaluated.

sections.title: Wall Settlement
sections.summary: Covers the causes and control of settlement in deep excavation wall systems. Earth pressure and inclined support forces have vertical components that can cause wall settlement, destressing tiebacks, and stressing bracing. Guidance is given for bearing layer requirements for different wall types, and references Chapter 6 for movement estimates when no bearing stratum is present.
sections.body:
Earth pressure forces and inclined support system forces have vertical components that can cause settlement of deep excavation wall systems. Wall settlement can cause destressing of tiebacks and stressing of internal bracing systems. Wall settlement must be considered and controlled, because wall design methods typically assume no vertical movement or settlement of the wall.

With the exception of sheet piling or combined sheet piling, the wall system should be driven, drilled, or excavated to a suitable bearing layer to avoid excessive wall settlement. For sheet piling or combined sheet piling, settlement can be reduced by driving or drilling sufficient sheet piles (e.g., every 5th pile) to a suitable bearing stratum. If a bearing stratum is not present, estimates of wall movement should be made using the methods of Chapter 6, and efforts should be made to reduce the vertical component of the support system forces.
key_points: Vertical components of earth pressure and inclined support forces can cause wall settlement.
Wall settlement can destress tiebacks and increase stress in internal bracing systems.
Most wall types should be installed to a suitable bearing layer to avoid excessive settlement.
For sheet piling, driving selected piles (e.g., every 5th pile) to a bearing stratum can reduce settlement.
When no bearing stratum exists, use Chapter 6 methods to estimate wall movement and minimize vertical force components.
sections.applicability: Applies when designing deep excavation walls with inclined or tieback support systems where vertical force components may induce wall settlement.

sections.title: Global Stability
sections.summary: Addresses deep-seated global stability analysis for excavations, requiring evaluation of failure surfaces below the wall and behind ground anchors. Surface surcharges, adjacent building loads, berms, and slopes must all be included. References DM 7.1 Chapter 7 for analysis methods and notes that rock excavations may require toe bolting for adversely oriented discontinuities.
sections.body:
Deep excavation design should consider the possibility of deep seated stability below the wall and behind any ground anchors. The stability analyses should consider surface loads from surcharges or adjacent buildings. If there are any berms or slopes in the system, these must also be considered. The stability analyses should be performed using the methods described in Chapter 7 of DM 7.1.

Excavations in rock below the wall may require rock bolting at the toe if bedding or adversely oriented joints dip into excavation or the rock surface slopes into excavation.
key_points: Global stability analyses must consider deep-seated failure surfaces below the wall and behind ground anchors.
Surcharges and adjacent building loads must be included in stability analyses.
Berms and slopes within or adjacent to the excavation system must also be evaluated.
Use DM 7.1 Chapter 7 methods for stability analyses.
Rock excavations may need toe rock bolting if bedding or joints dip into the excavation or the rock surface slopes inward.
sections.applicability: Applies to all deep excavation designs where deep-seated failure, ground anchors, surcharges, slopes, or rock discontinuities may influence stability.

sections.title: Basal Instability or Heave
sections.summary: Covers analysis of basal heave in deep excavations, primarily a concern where excavation width exceeds depth in soft to medium clays. Presents the normalized wall stiffness parameter (Kwall) from Mana and Clough (1981) for distinguishing flexible vs. stiff wall behavior, a required FS ≥ 1.5, and references Figure 2-7 for calculation methods for both coarse-grained soils and clays.
sections.body:
Basal heave is the tendency of the bottom of an excavation to move upward because of the weight of the soil adjacent to the excavation. Basal heave in deep excavations is usually only an issue where the width of excavation (B) is greater than depth (H). It is primarily a concern for soft to medium clays that extend to significant depth.

A method for calculating basal instability of braced excavations in coarse-grained soils is provided in Figure 2-7(a). Basal instability is less common in coarse-grained soils than clays.

For clays, the method used to calculate the factor of safety against basal heave (FBH) depends on the relative wall flexibility. Flexible walls (e.g., sheet piling) will deform with the soil, and the portion of the wall that penetrates below the base of the excavation is ignored. Stiff walls (e.g., concrete diaphragm) prevent the soil from deflecting toward the base of the excavation. The soil must flow beneath the wall and up towards the base of the excavation for heave to occur. Thus, for stiff walls, the wall penetration below the base is considered. A factor of safety of at least 1.5 should be used against basal heave failure as discussed by Mana and Clough (1981). The normalized wall stiffness, Kwall, as defined by Mana and Clough (1981) can be found as:

Kwall = EI / (γt × h^4)

where:
E = Young's modulus of wall,
I = second moment of the area of the wall section (I = t³ / 12 for wall thickness t),
γt = total unit weight of the retained soil, and
h = vertical spacing of the support system braces or anchors.

The normalized wall stiffness is greatly influenced by the spacing of the support system, because this variable is raised to the fourth power. A secondary consideration is the movement required to mobilize the support system. Ground anchors and internal bracing can be prestressed to reduce mobilization movement. In contrast, soil nails require movement to develop support forces.

The calculation of basal heave for clays is shown in Figure 2-7(b) and (c). For flexible walls, the driving force is the weight of the soil extending a distance, B1, beyond the excavation plus the surcharge loading. The resisting force is developed along the sides of the block of soil defined by B1 and in the soil below the excavation.

For very stiff walls, the shear resistance in the clay along the inside of the wall may be included. An adhesion factor (α) between the wall and clay is multiplied by the undrained strength of the clay in this layer. Very stiff walls are much more effective at reducing lateral movement and basal heave than flexible walls, producing the higher factors of safety against basal heave.
key_points: Basal heave is primarily a concern when excavation width (B) > depth (H) in soft to medium clays.
A minimum factor of safety of 1.5 against basal heave is required (Mana and Clough, 1981).
Normalized wall stiffness Kwall = EI/(γt·h⁴); brace/anchor spacing h has the dominant influence (raised to 4th power).
Flexible walls (e.g., sheet piling): wall penetration below excavation base is ignored in FBH calculation.
Stiff walls (e.g., concrete diaphragm): wall penetration is considered; soil must flow beneath wall for heave to occur.
Very stiff walls may include wall-clay adhesion (factor α × Su) to increase resistance against basal heave.
Soil nails require movement to develop support forces, unlike prestressed anchors or internal bracing.
Figure 2-7 provides calculation methods for both coarse-grained soils (a) and clays (b, c).

equations.description: Normalized wall stiffness Kwall = EI / (γt × h⁴), where E = Young's modulus of wall, I = second moment of area of wall section (t³/12 for thickness t), γt = total unit weight of retained soil, h = vertical spacing of support system braces or anchors.

figures: Figure 2-7 — Methods for Calculating Factor of Safety Against Basal Instability or Heave (after Wong and Goh 2002): (a) coarse-grained soils, (b) flexible walls in clay, (c) stiff walls in clay
sections.applicability: Applies when evaluating basal heave potential for deep excavations in soft to medium clays or coarse-grained soils, particularly where excavation width exceeds depth.

sections.title: Ground Movements Adjacent to Deep Excavations
sections.summary: Introduces procedures for estimating maximum horizontal and vertical movements adjacent to deep excavation support walls, profiles of movement with distance from the wall, and methods to predict damage to adjacent structures. Covers three soil categories: stiff clays/sands/residual soils, and soft to medium clays, updating Peck (1969) with Clough and O'Rourke (1990) methods.
sections.body:
Prediction of wall movement is an important part of the design of deep excavation systems. This section presents procedures to estimate (1) the anticipated maximum horizontal or lateral movements and the maximum settlement immediately behind the excavation support wall, (2) the profile of movement with distance from the wall, and (3) methods to predict damage to structures adjacent to excavations.

Observations of settlement behind sheet piling walls and soldier pile (H-pile) and lagging walls in the mid-20th century suggested the trends shown in Figure 2-8 (Peck 1969). The settlement (δV) and distance from the wall (d) are both normalized by the depth of excavation (H). The movements shown in Figure 2-8 were state of the practice in the late 1960s and can occur today with poor construction workmanship or by lowering the groundwater during construction, which may increase the load on the wall. Peck separated typical movements into three zones of interest based on soil type and basal stability:

- Zone I – Sand and hard clays (limited soft clay): FBH > 2
- Zone II – Soft clays below excavation: 1 < FBH < 2
- Zone III – Soft clays to significant depth below excavation: FBH ≈ 1

Control of movements has improved in deep excavations. New methods of support and new walls have been introduced since Peck developed Figure 2-8. Clough and O'Rourke (1990) updated Peck's approach and attempted to screen projects to remove movements that were not primarily related to the excavation support processes (O'Rourke 1981, Mana and Clough 1981, Clough et al. 1989). This section presents the subject in the following categories:
- Maximum movements of excavation support walls in stiff clays, sands and residual soils;
- Profiles of movements beyond excavation support walls in stiff to hard clays and sands; and
- Maximum movements of excavation support walls and profiles of movements beyond excavation support walls in soft to medium clays.

Typical values of settlement and horizontal movement at the wall are summarized in Table 2-8. The values are presented as a percentage of the excavation depth (H). The lateral extent of movement is also summarized as a ratio compared to H.
key_points: Peck (1969) defined three settlement zones based on soil type and factor of safety against basal heave (FBH > 2, 1 < FBH < 2, FBH ≈ 1).
Clough and O'Rourke (1990) updated Peck's approach, screening out movements not related to excavation support processes.
Movements are normalized by excavation depth H; typical values of δVm/H and δHm/H are summarized in Table 2-8.
Three soil categories are addressed: stiff clays/sands/residual soils, and soft to medium clays.
Lateral extent of movement is also expressed as a ratio d/H, ranging from 1.5 to 3 depending on soil type and wall stiffness.
Poor construction workmanship or groundwater lowering can result in movements equivalent to 1960s practice.
sections.applicability: Applies when estimating ground movements and settlement profiles adjacent to any deep excavation support system, for all soil types.

sections.title: Movements in Stiff Clays, Sands, and Residual Soils
sections.summary: Presents case history-based methods for estimating maximum lateral and vertical wall movements in stiff clays, sands, and residual soils. Establishes that δVm averages 0.15%·H and δHm averages 0.2%·H, both ranging up to 0.5%·H, and that wall type has little effect on movement magnitude. Finite element analyses confirm the importance of soil modulus and K0 over wall stiffness.
sections.body:
Based on case histories of walls in these soils, the maximum horizontal (lateral) movement (δHm) and the maximum settlement (δVm) vary approximately linearly with excavation depth as shown in Figure 2-9 (Clough and O'Rourke 1990). This suggests that the retained soil masses behave approximately as an elastic material. The maximum settlement is presented in Figure 2-9(a) and indicates that the average δVm was about 0.15%·H and ranged up to about 0.5%·H. Figure 2-9(b) presents the maximum lateral movement and indicates that the average δHm was about 0.2%·H and also ranged up to about 0.5%·H.

The points with very large movements likely relate to factors other than the support system, such as lowered groundwater or poor construction practices. Some of these points would plot in Zones II and III of Figure 2-8 at d/H = 0. The ground movements below the 0.5%H lines can be attributed to movement of the support system and not extraneous factors.

Two important concepts are illustrated in Figure 2-9. The horizontal movement data is more scattered than the settlement data. In addition, there are no significant differences in the data for different types of wall construction (e.g., sheet piling, soldier pile (H-pile) and lagging, diaphragm, drilled piers, deep soil mix).

Clough and O'Rourke (1990) used finite element analyses to confirm the δHm = 0.2%·H trend line indicated by the data in Figure 2-9(b). The effects of soil modulus (Es), normalized wall stiffness (Kwall), support spacing (h), and coefficient of lateral earth pressure (K0) on wall movements were also studied. K0 accounts for the higher horizontal earth pressures found in overconsolidated soils. The finite element analyses, which considered the elastic nature of these relatively stiff soils, found that:
- Es and K0 generally had a greater impact on wall δHm than wall stiffness,
- Higher Es and lower K0 yielded lower δHm, and
- Lower Es and higher K0 yielded higher δHm.

In these cases, the soil was stiff enough to minimize the influence of wall stiffness. Figure 2-9 can be used to estimate δHm and δVm of new excavation support systems in stiff clays, sands, and residual soils.
key_points: Average δVm ≈ 0.15%·H and average δHm ≈ 0.2%·H; both range up to 0.5%·H in stiff clays, sands, and residual soils.
Movements exceeding 0.5%·H are likely related to extraneous factors such as groundwater lowering or poor construction.
Wall type (sheet piling, soldier pile, diaphragm, deep soil mix) has no significant effect on δHm or δVm in these soils.
Soil modulus (Es) and K0 have greater influence on δHm than wall stiffness in stiff soils.
Higher Es and lower K0 reduce δHm; lower Es and higher K0 increase δHm.
The retained soil mass behaves approximately elastically, leading to a near-linear movement vs. depth relationship.
sections.applicability: Applies when estimating maximum lateral and vertical wall movements for excavations in stiff clays, sands, and residual (Piedmont/Blue Ridge) soils.

sections.title: Profiles of Movement in Stiff to Hard Clays
sections.summary: Presents dimensionless settlement and horizontal movement profiles for excavations in stiff to hard clays, based on case histories with various wall and bracing systems. Average δVm ≈ 0.15%·H and δHm ≈ 0.2%·H; movements decrease to negligible at d/H = 3.0. High-K0 overconsolidated clays may experience large lateral stress relief and anchor movement issues.
sections.body:
Figure 2-10 summarizes case histories for stiff to hard clays. The wall and bracing systems include soldier piles and lagging with tieback anchors, concrete diaphragm walls with tieback anchors, concrete diaphragm walls with cross lot struts, drilled shaft walls and tieback anchors, and walls with internal raker braces. For more information on specific data points, see Clough and O'Rourke (1990).

Settlements: Figure 2-10 indicates that δVm ranged from 0% to 0.3%·H and averaged about 0.15%·H. This average maximum settlement is consistent with Figure 2-9(a). The settlement decreased from the wall to negligible values at d/H = 3.0 where d is the distance from the face of the excavation support wall. A few of the cases experienced heave due to stress relief experienced by the stiff to very hard clays surrounding the deep excavations. The dimensionless settlement profile (Figure 2-10(c)) may be used to estimate the vertical movement pattern adjacent to an excavation in stiff to hard clay.

Horizontal Movements: Two categories of horizontal movement are shown in Figure 2-10(b). Support systems with high horizontal stiffness reduce movement, resulting in a δHm of about 0.3%·H. An average value of δHm = 0.2%·H is appropriate for most estimates, which is similar to the typical trend shown in Figure 2-9(b). Support systems with low horizontal stiffness allow increased movement, and the maximum lateral movement is up to 0.8%·H. Similar to the settlement profile, a triangular horizontal movement profile can be used to estimate the horizontal movement with δH decreasing to a negligible value at d/H = 3.0.

Very stiff to hard clays and shales may have high in situ K0 in the range of 2 to 3. The value of K0 can be estimated from the overconsolidation ratio and friction angle (see Equation 4-2). Excavations in these materials may induce lateral stress relief and large lateral movement. Anchors in these materials may move with the soil if not installed beyond the zone of movement, which can conservatively be assumed to extend up from the base of the excavation at an angle of 45° from horizontal.
key_points: δVm ranges from 0% to 0.3%·H, averaging 0.15%·H; settlements decrease to negligible at d/H = 3.0.
δHm averages 0.2%·H for most systems; high-stiffness systems yield ~0.3%·H, low-stiffness systems up to 0.8%·H.
Triangular movement profile is recommended for both settlement and horizontal movement in stiff to hard clay.
Some cases show heave due to stress relief in very stiff to hard clays surrounding deep excavations.
High-K0 overconsolidated clays (K0 = 2 to 3) may develop large lateral movements from stress relief.
Anchors must be installed beyond the zone of movement (conservatively 45° from base of excavation) to avoid moving with the soil.
sections.applicability: Applies when estimating settlement and horizontal movement profiles adjacent to excavations in stiff to hard clay soils.

sections.title: Profiles of Movement in Sands
sections.summary: Presents dimensionless settlement and horizontal movement profiles for excavations in sand and sand-gravel profiles based on Clough and O'Rourke (1990) case histories. Maximum δVm is typically less than 0.3%·H, averaging 0.1–0.2%·H, and movements decrease to negligible at d/H = 2.0, which is shorter than in stiff clays.
sections.body:
Figure 2-11 summarizes case histories for subsurface profiles consisting of sand or sand and gravel with limited clay layers (Clough and O'Rourke 1990). Groundwater was either lowered, or recharged to reduce settlement, but did not vary during construction. The wall systems include both flexible and stiff walls, including soldier piles and lagging with cross lot struts or tieback anchors, sheet piling with tieback anchors, and concrete diaphragm walls with cross lot struts.

Settlements: The maximum settlement tends to be less than 0.3%·H in sand and decreases to a negligible value at d/H = 2.0. In the majority of cases, the range of δVm was about 0.1%·H to 0.2%·H and averaged about 0.15%H, which may be used to estimate the maximum settlement. The dimensionless settlement profile in Figure 2-11(b) may be used to estimate the vertical movement pattern adjacent to an excavation in sand.

Horizontal Movements: Clough and O'Rourke (1990) do not give specific recommendations for horizontal movement in excavations made in sand. For sand, the average value of δHm = 0.2%·H can be used from Figure 2-9(b). Horizontal movements are expected to decrease to negligible values at d/H = 2.0 with a horizontal movement profile similar to the settlement profile in Figure 2-11(b).
key_points: δVm is typically less than 0.3%·H in sand, averaging 0.1–0.2%·H; movements become negligible at d/H = 2.0.
The influence zone in sand (d/H = 2.0) is shorter than in stiff to hard clay (d/H = 3.0).
δHm = 0.2%·H (from Figure 2-9(b)) is recommended for sand; no specific case history recommendations exist from Clough and O'Rourke (1990).
The horizontal movement profile in sand is assumed similar to the settlement profile in Figure 2-11(b).
Groundwater control (lowering or recharging) was maintained constant during construction for the case history data.
sections.applicability: Applies when estimating settlement and horizontal movement profiles adjacent to excavations in sand or sand-gravel profiles.

sections.title: Movements in Soft to Medium Clays
sections.summary: Presents case history-based methods for estimating maximum lateral and vertical movements adjacent to excavations in soft to medium clays. δVm is limited to 2%·H with a trapezoidal settlement profile extending to d/H = 1.5–2.0. Horizontal movements are governed by the factor of safety against basal heave and normalized wall stiffness, as shown in Figure 2-13 finite element curves.
sections.body:
Figure 2-12 summarizes case histories of wall movements in soft to medium clays (Mana and Clough 1981, Clough et al. 1989, Clough and O'Rourke 1990). The types of wall and bracing systems were sheet piling with cross lot struts, soldier piles and lagging with cross lot struts, and concrete diaphragm walls with cross lot struts. On some projects, berms and rakers were used as full or supplemental support. The Peck (1969) zones are included on Figure 2-12(a) for reference.

Settlements: The maximum settlements are limited to about 2%·H and have a trapezoidal profile behind the wall as shown in Figure 2-12(a). The trapezoidal profile extends at δVm = 2%·H from the wall to d/H = 0.75 and then slopes up to δV = 0.0 at d/H = 1.5 where settlements decreased to negligible values. In most cases, the settlement was less than 1%·H. When reasonable care is used during construction and the factor of safety against basal heave is about 2, δVm = 1%·H may be assumed. This is true for either flexible or stiff excavation support walls, provided large cantilever movements are limited. When excavation support walls are flexible and the factor of safety against basal heave is less than 1.5, δVm = 2%·H is a reasonable assumption.

The settlements are normalized by δVm in Figure 2-12(b). The settlements fall within a trapezoidal region that extends to zero at d/H of about 1.5 or can conservatively be extended to d/H = 2 as proposed by Clough and O'Rourke.

Horizontal Movements: The case history data of δHm / H for soft to medium clays are plotted against normalized wall stiffness in Figure 2-13 for sheet piling and slurry concrete diaphragm walls. The overall wall stability increased as the basal factor of safety is increased as shown in Figure 2-13. For soft to medium clays, horizontal movements are highly dependent on the factor of safety against basal heave. The stiff diaphragm walls generally had a factor of safety greater than 2. The more flexible sheet piling walls had a factor of safety generally less than 1.5 except where the subsurface conditions were favorable to a stable base.

Figure 2-13 also presents the results of finite element analyses by Clough and O'Rourke (1990), which match the case history data well. The finite element curves can be used to select δHm / H based on normalized wall stiffness and factor of safety against basal heave for excavations in soft to medium clays. Note that the normalized wall stiffness is greatly influenced by spacing of the bracing or anchors (h). The range of normalized wall stiffness used in the finite element analyses are shown at the top of Figure 2-13 where the bracing was set at h = 3.5 m or about 12 feet, which is a typical design spacing.

The profile of horizontal movements for soft clays is likely similar to that observed for settlements. Thus, a dimensionless horizontal movement profile similar to that shown in Figure 2-12 for settlement may be assumed for soft to medium clays.
key_points: Maximum settlement in soft to medium clay is limited to 2%·H with a trapezoidal profile; most cases are below 1%·H.
Trapezoidal settlement profile extends at δVm from wall to d/H = 0.75, then decreases to zero at d/H = 1.5 (or 2.0 conservatively).
With FBH ≈ 2 and good construction practice, δVm = 1%·H is appropriate; with flexible walls and FBH < 1.5, assume δVm = 2%·H.
Horizontal movements are highly dependent on FBH and normalized wall stiffness (Kwall); use Figure 2-13 finite element curves to estimate δHm/H.
Stiff diaphragm walls typically achieve FBH > 2; flexible sheet piling walls typically have FBH < 1.5.
The horizontal movement profile in soft to medium clay is assumed similar to the trapezoidal settlement profile.
sections.applicability: Applies when estimating maximum lateral and vertical movements, and their profiles, adjacent to excavations in soft to medium clay soils.

sections.title: Prediction of Damage to Adjacent Structures
sections.summary: Provides methods to assess damage potential to structures adjacent to deep excavations using angular distortion (β) and horizontal strain (εh). Introduces Equations 2-3 through 2-6 for computing β and εh and for estimating movements at any point behind the wall. Uses Figure 2-14 (after Boscardin and Cording 1989) to map predicted deformations to damage categories. Discusses underpinning methods in Table 2-9.
sections.body:
The movements of braced or anchored deep excavation support systems should be evaluated to determine if adjacent structures supported by shallow foundations require underpinning. The distance of existing structures from the excavation support system should be compared to the movement profiles in Figure 2-10 to Figure 2-12. Tolerance of structures to movement is discussed in Chapter 5 of DM 7.1. Other factors that influence the need for underpinning include:
- Lowering groundwater by dewatering may cause soil consolidation and settlement.
- Soldier piles and lagging, sheet piling, and tangent piles all leak to various degrees, and this will lower groundwater.
- Leaks in the excavation support system can also cause loss of fines, piping, and settlement if not properly filtered.

The predicted angular distortion, β, and the horizontal strain, εh, across the building can be used to assess damage potential. Angular distortion is the differential vertical movement between two points divided by distance separating the points (Eq. 2-3). Similarly, horizontal strain (εh) between two points is given by Eq. 2-4.

In most cases, β and εh will be measured across the whole building width. In this case, the movements would be estimated at the front and back of the building (compared to the excavation), and db would equal the building width. The movements may be estimated from δVm, δHm, and the movement profile behind the wall, which are found using the methods in Sections 2-4.4.1 and 2-4.4.2.

For stiff to hard clays and sands, the movements can be estimated using Eq. 2-5, where δi is the desired horizontal or vertical movement at the point of interest, δm is the maximum movement at the wall, di is the distance from wall to the point of interest, and d0 = 3H for stiff to hard clays and 2H for sand.

For soft to medium clays, movements can be estimated using Eq. 2-6, with different expressions depending on whether di/H is between 0.75 and 1.5, or between 1.5 and 0.75.

A method to evaluate the severity of damage from excavations to adjacent structures based on β and εh is presented in Figure 2-14 (Clough and O'Rourke 1990). Figure 2-14 maps damage categories for masonry load-bearing wall structures to predicted values of horizontal strain and angular distortion (Boscardin and Cording 1989). The damage categories are negligible, very slight, slight, moderate to severe, and severe to very severe. This damage mapping is based on theoretical structural response to deformation, field observations of building damage, and measurement of building horizontal and vertical displacements. When β ≈ 0, the boundaries for the categories are nearly horizontal and represent horizontal tensile strains that equal the critical tensile strains. When εh ≈ 0, the boundaries are inclined at about 45° and represent diagonal tensile strains that equal the critical tensile strains.

The estimated ratio of horizontal to vertical movements at the edge of the excavation may be estimated from δHm and δVm. These ratios are expected to be uniform from the wall to a distance of d = 0.5H. Ratios of δHm / δVm are superimposed for stiff soil types in Figure 2-14(a) and for soft to medium clays in Figure 2-14(b) (Clough and O'Rourke 1990, O'Rourke 1981). The ratios are based on the data analyzed in Figure 2-10 to Figure 2-13. In sands and stiff to hard clays, damage typically is bounded by the moderate to severe level, and construction controls can diminish the severity of movement. In soft to medium clays, damage typically is bounded by severe to very severe level, and insufficiently stiff bracing can result in additional movement.

If estimated movements are too large as indicated by Figure 2-14 for the existing structure to tolerate, underpinning will be required. Underpinning methods are described in FHWA (1978). Since underpinning may be required for adjacent buildings when considering deep excavation support systems, underpinning methods are discussed in Table 2-9. Example problems considering the topic of deep excavation support systems are presented in Figure 2-15 for stiff to hard clay and in Figure 2-16 for soft to medium clay.
key_points: Angular distortion β = (δVi − δVj) / db and horizontal strain εh = (δHi − δHj) / db are used to assess building damage potential (Eq. 2-3, Eq. 2-4).
For stiff to hard clays and sands, movement at any distance is estimated by linear interpolation from the wall (d0 = 3H for clay, 2H for sand) using Eq. 2-5.
For soft to medium clays, a trapezoidal movement profile is used with the piecewise expression in Eq. 2-6.
Figure 2-14 maps β and εh to five damage categories (negligible to severe/very severe) for masonry load-bearing structures.
In stiff soils, damage is typically bounded by moderate to severe; in soft to medium clays, damage can reach severe to very severe.
Groundwater lowering, wall leakage, and loss of fines are additional factors that may necessitate underpinning beyond what movement profiles suggest.
Common underpinning methods include micropiles, jacked H-piles/pipe piles, helical piers, and underpinning pits (Table 2-9).

equations.description: Angular distortion β between two building points i and j: β = (δVi − δVj) / db, where δVi and δVj are estimated settlements at points i and j, and db is the distance separating the points.
Horizontal strain εh between two building points: εh = (δHi − δHj) / db, where δHi and δHj are estimated horizontal movements at two points, and db is the distance separating the points.

Movement at a point of interest for stiff to hard clays and sands: δi = δm · (1 − di/d0), where δm is the maximum movement at the wall, di is distance from wall to point of interest, and d0 = 3H for stiff to hard clays and 2H for sand.
Movement at a point of interest for soft to medium clays: δi = δm for di/H ≤ 0.75; δi = δm · (1.5 − di/H) / (1.5 − 0.75) for 0.75 ≤ di/H ≤ 1.5 (trapezoidal profile).

sections.applicability: Applies when evaluating potential damage to adjacent structures due to ground movements from deep excavations, and determining whether underpinning is required.

sections.title: Construction Considerations
sections.summary: Covers how construction procedures affect deep excavation support system movements, referencing Table 2-10 which details construction considerations and comments for wall and support system elements including sheet piles, soldier piles and lagging, combined sheet piles, secant/tangent piles, and deep soil mixing. FHWA (2008) is cited for additional guidance.
sections.body: Construction procedures can have an impact on deep excavation support system movements. Table 2-10 lists many of the construction considerations for various wall and support system features. FHWA (2008) provides additional guidance.
key_points: Construction procedures directly influence movements in deep excavation support systems.
Sheet pile driving considerations include interlock separation (primary cause of seepage/piping), groundwater lowering effects, and vibratory hammer-induced settlement in loose to medium sands.
Soldier pile and lagging systems require care in driven or predrilled installation; lagging is typically 3 inches thick and should be removed above the water table after construction.
Combined sheet pile walls require special interlocks and critical vertical alignment between sheet piles and king piles.
Secant and tangent pile walls require a reinforced concrete guide wall (3–5 ft deep) and careful concrete placement; tangent piles carry higher risk of groundwater leakage.
Deep soil mixing walls rely on in situ soil, requiring removal of obstructions, monitoring of mixing operations, and test columns; extraneous material must not enter production columns.
FHWA (2008) provides additional guidance beyond Table 2-10 for all wall types.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting and executing construction methods for deep excavation support systems, including sheet pile, soldier pile, combined sheet pile, secant/tangent pile, and deep soil mixing walls.

sections.title: Rock Excavations
sections.summary: Covers planning, design, and construction considerations for rock excavations, including preliminary investigation requirements, assessment of excavation methods (mechanical and blasting), and blasting design/monitoring. Addresses factors such as geological structure, in situ stresses, groundwater, rippability, and effects on adjacent structures.
key_points: Rock excavation planning requires detailed field investigations: review of available data, geological mapping, and test borings to define stratigraphy.
Infrastructure in rock should be oriented favorably with geological structure (e.g., tunnel axes perpendicular to fault strike).
Key factors include fault/fracture orientation, in situ stresses, groundwater, joint fill, slope geometry, dynamic loading, weathering rate, rippability, and blasting effects.
DM 7.1 Chapters 1–7 provide supplementary guidance on rock description, classification, testing, stress, seepage, and slope stability.
sections.applicability: Applies to all projects involving excavation in rock, from preliminary planning through construction.
