sections.title: Preliminary Considerations
sections.summary: Outlines the essential preliminary steps and factors for rock excavation planning and design. Requires detailed field investigations (data review, geological mapping, test borings) and favorable orientation of infrastructure relative to geological structure. Lists ten key factors—including faults, in situ stresses, groundwater, rippability, and blasting effects—that govern excavation planning.
key_points: Field investigations must include review of existing data, geological mapping of exposed rock, and test borings to define stratigraphy.
Align tunnels with axes perpendicular to fault strike; avoid downslope dip of discontinuities into open excavations.

Ten critical factors govern rock excavation design: faults/fractures, in situ stresses, groundwater, joint fill, cut geometry, sliding surfaces, dynamic loading, weathering rate, rippability, and blasting effects on adjacent structures.
DM 7.1 (Chapters 1–4, 6–7) is the primary supplementary reference for rock description, classification, testing, stress, seepage, and slope stability.
sections.applicability: Applies during planning and design phases of any rock excavation project.

sections.title: Assessment of Rock Excavation Methods
sections.summary: Describes methods for evaluating the most appropriate rock excavation technique—excavators, rippers, hoe rams, or blasting. Covers three approaches: field test sections, GSI-based excavatability correlations, and seismic compression wave velocity correlations. Selection depends on rock mass characteristics, equipment capability, and project geometry.
sections.body: Rock excavation can be accomplished by excavators, rippers, hoe rams, and blasting. The following paragraphs discuss how to evaluate which of these methods are most appropriate.
key_points: Rock excavation methods include power excavators, rippers (D8/D9/D11 tractors), hoe rams, and blasting.
Method selection is evaluated through field test sections, GSI correlations, and seismic P-wave velocity correlations.
The size and shape of the excavation area significantly affects rippability estimates.
Equipment manufacturer charts (e.g., Caterpillar) relate P-wave velocity to ripper performance for medium, heavy, and very heavy tractors.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting the appropriate excavation method for a rock excavation project during design and planning.

sections.title: Rock Excavatability Based on Rock Test Sections
sections.summary: Describes the use of field rock test sections during the design phase to evaluate excavation equipment performance. Various equipment types (excavators, rippers, hoe rams) are tested on-site to determine effective depth of ripping/excavation and to identify where blasting will be required. The size and shape of the excavation area are key factors in rippability estimation.
sections.body: The field observation of a rock test section is helpful during the design phase of a project. Various types of equipment, such as excavators, rippers, and hoe rams, can be tested to evaluate which type of equipment would be most effective during construction. The size and shape of the area to be excavated is a significant factor in estimating the ability to rip rock. This exploration technique will provide valuable data on the depth that can be ripped or excavated with each type of equipment and will also define where and at what depth blasting will be required.
key_points: Field test sections during the design phase allow direct comparison of excavator, ripper, and hoe ram performance.
Test sections define the maximum rippable/excavatable depth for each equipment type and identify zones requiring blasting.
The size and shape of the excavation area is a significant factor in rippability estimation.
sections.applicability: Applies during the design phase of rock excavation projects where direct field evaluation of equipment performance is feasible.

sections.title: Rock Excavatability Based on Correlations with GSI
sections.summary: Presents a method for assessing rock excavatability using the Geologic Strength Index (GSI), which is assigned based on rock mass structure and surface condition. Uses Figure 2-17 (after Tsiambaos and Saroglou 2010) with shaded zones distinguishing digging, ripping, hammer/blasting, and blasting-only regions, split by point load strength index Is(50) threshold of 31 tsf (3 MPa).
sections.body: The excavatability of rock by various methods can be related to Geologic Strength Index (GSI) (Hoek et al. 1992, Marinos and Hoek 2000). The GSI is assigned based on the rock mass structure and the surface condition as shown by the numbered contours in Figure 2-17. Tsiambaos and Saroglou (2010) split sedimentary and metamorphic rock masses ranging from blocky to disintegrated into two groups by point load strength index (Is(50)). The region corresponding to the rock's structure and surface conditions can be determined. The shaded areas indicate different levels of excavatability. Digging means the rock can be excavated with power excavators. Ripping indicates excavation with D8 and D9 type tractors. Hammer (and blasting) means that breaking with a hoe or hydraulic ram will likely be required. Blasting indicates the need for blasting.
key_points: GSI is determined from rock mass structure and surface condition using Figure 2-17.
Tsiambaos and Saroglou (2010) divide rock masses into two groups by point load strength index Is(50): < 31 tsf (3 MPa) and > 31 tsf (3 MPa).
Four excavatability categories: Digging (power excavators), Ripping (D8/D9 tractors), Hammer/Blasting (hoe or hydraulic ram), and Blasting.
Applies to sedimentary and metamorphic rock masses ranging from blocky to disintegrated structure.
figures: Figure 2-17 Excavatability of Rock Masses: a) Is(50) < 31 tsf (3 MPa) and b) Is(50) > 31 tsf (3 MPa) (after Tsiambaos and Saroglou 2010)
sections.applicability: Applies when assessing rock excavatability using GSI for sedimentary and metamorphic rock masses during design.

sections.title: Rippability Based on Correlations with Compression Wave Velocity
sections.summary: Describes assessment of rock rippability using seismic P-wave (compression wave) velocity from seismic refraction studies. Rippability depends on lithology, fracture condition and orientation, weathering, rock strength, and ripper equipment size. Figure 2-18 (Caterpillar 2000) provides example charts correlating P-wave velocity to ripper performance for D-8, D-9, and D-11 tractors.
sections.body:
Ripping of rock materials is governed by many factors: 1) rock mass lithology including strata, fracture condition, and orientation; 2) rock weathering; 3) rock strength; and 4) rock ripper equipment size and condition. Rock rippability can be assessed from field observation and correlations with the GSI as discussed above or by using correlations with seismic wave velocity.

The most common rock rippability correlation is based on compression wave velocity, or P-wave velocity, obtained from seismic refraction studies. The velocity is based on the fracture condition of the rock. Figure 2-18 illustrates example charts for the performance of rippers mounted on medium (Caterpillar D-8 tractor), heavy (D-9 tractor), and very heavy-duty (D-11 tractor) tractors related to seismic compression wave velocity of various rock materials (Caterpillar 2000). These types of charts are available from equipment manufacturers.
key_points: Rock rippability is governed by lithology/fracture condition, rock weathering, rock strength, and equipment size/condition.
The most common rippability correlation uses P-wave velocity from seismic refraction studies; velocity reflects the fracture condition of the rock.
Figure 2-18 provides Caterpillar charts correlating P-wave velocity to ripper performance for D-8 (medium), D-9 (heavy), and D-11 (very heavy-duty) tractors.
Equipment manufacturer charts are a standard resource for rippability assessment.
figures: Figure 2-18 Ripper Performance: a) Medium Tractor, b) Heavy-Duty Tractor, and c) Very Heavy Tractors (after Caterpillar 2000)
sections.applicability: Applies when assessing rippability of rock using seismic refraction P-wave velocity data during design or exploration phases.

sections.title: Blasting
sections.summary: Covers blasting requirements for rock excavation once mechanical methods are insufficient. Requires a pre-blasting survey including site examination, photographic record of adjacent structures, and establishment of survey control points. Includes subsections on blasting design using scaled distance and peak particle velocity (PPV) and on construction-phase monitoring protocols.
sections.body: Once it has been determined that blasting is required, a pre-blasting survey should be performed. As a minimum, this should include: 1) examination of the site, 2) detailed examination and a photographic record of adjacent structures, and 3) establishment of horizontal and vertical survey control points.
key_points: A pre-blasting survey is mandatory before any blasting begins: site examination, photographic record of adjacent structures, and survey control points.
Blasting design is based on scaled distance (SD) and peak particle velocity (PPV) criteria.
PPV is the accepted criterion for evaluating potential structural damage from blasting vibration.
Construction-phase monitoring uses vibration stations with detailed records of charge weight, location, distance, delays, and structural response.
sections.applicability: Applies when blasting has been determined to be necessary for rock excavation on a project.

sections.title: Blasting Design
sections.summary: Presents the quantitative framework for blasting design using scaled distance (SD) and peak particle velocity (PPV). Defines SD as true distance corrected by charge weight (Eq. 2-7), and PPV as a function of SD with empirical confinement factor K (Eq. 2-8, 2-9). Figures 2-19 and 2-20 enable estimation of structural damage potential and human response to vibration.
sections.body:
Design of blasting for a project can be estimated by considering the maximum particle velocity. The peak (or maximum) particle velocity (PPV) is the longitudinal velocity of a particle in the direction of the wave that is generated by blasting. The major concern in blasting is the influence of the blasting on adjacent structures. PPV is an accepted criterion for evaluating the potential for structural damage induced by blasting vibration. The critical level of the particle velocity depends on the rock properties, the nature of the overburden, the frequency characteristics of the structure, and the capability of the structure to withstand dynamic stresses.

The effects of a blast on a structure can be evaluated by the scaled distance (USBM 1971, Oriard 1987). The scaled distance (SD) is the true distance from the charge to the structure corrected by the weight of the charge and can be calculated as:

SD = D / W^β

where:
D = true distance from charge to structure (ft),
W = weight of charge (lb), and
β = 0.33 for near field structures (i.e., <20 ft from charge) or 0.5 further from charge.

The scaled distance is not correct dimensionally and requires use of the indicated units.

Using SD, the PPV can be estimated using:

PPV = K · SD^(−1.6)

where:
K = confinement factor (lower bound = 20, upper bound = 242, average = 150).

The values of K are empirical and require the use of the indicated units. K may be calculated from blast data as follows:

K = PPV / SD^(−1.6)

Figure 2-19 can then be used to estimate potential damage to structures based on the estimated PPV. Human response to vibrations is given in Figure 2-20.
key_points: PPV (peak particle velocity) is the accepted criterion for evaluating blasting-induced structural damage risk.
Scaled distance SD = D / W^β; β = 0.33 for near-field (<20 ft) and 0.5 for far-field (Eq. 2-7). Units are ft and lb; equation is dimensionally inconsistent.
PPV = K · SD^(−1.6), where K is the empirical confinement factor (range 20–242, average 150) (Eq. 2-8).
K can be back-calculated from blast monitoring data as K = PPV / SD^(−1.6) (Eq. 2-9).
Figure 2-19 (Blast Effects Scale) maps PPV to structural damage potential; Figure 2-20 addresses human response to vibration.
Critical PPV level depends on rock properties, overburden nature, structural frequency characteristics, and dynamic stress capacity.

equations.description: Scaled distance SD = D / W^β, where D = true distance from charge to structure (ft), W = weight of charge (lb), and β = 0.33 for near-field structures (<20 ft) or 0.5 for structures further from the charge. Dimensionally inconsistent; use indicated units only.
Peak particle velocity PPV = K · SD^(−1.6), where K is the empirical confinement factor (lower bound = 20, upper bound = 242, average = 150). Empirical; use indicated units.
Back-calculation of confinement factor K from blast monitoring data: K = PPV / SD^(−1.6). Used to derive site-specific K values from measured PPV and scaled distance.

figures: Figure 2-19 Blast Effects Scale (after Konya and Walter 2006)
sections.applicability: Applies during blasting design to estimate scaled distance and peak particle velocity for evaluating potential structural damage and human response.

sections.title: Monitoring Blasting
sections.summary: Specifies requirements for construction-phase blasting vibration monitoring. Monitoring stations must be established, with detailed records of charge weight, blast location, distance to structures, delays, and vibration response. Small initial charges are used to develop a site-specific charge weight–distance–PPV relationship and assess associated structural response before larger blasts are executed.
sections.body: During construction, vibration monitoring stations should be established, and monitoring should be performed. Detailed records should be kept of charge weight, location of blast point, distance from blast point to existing structures, delays, and response as indicated by vibration monitoring. For safety, small charges should be used initially to establish a site-specific relationship between charge weight, distance, and peak particle velocity along with the associated structural response.
key_points: Vibration monitoring stations must be established during construction; monitoring is required throughout blasting operations.
Records must include charge weight, blast point location, distance to existing structures, delays, and measured vibration response.
Small initial charges should be used to develop a site-specific charge weight–distance–PPV relationship before full-scale blasting.
Site-specific K values derived from monitoring improve the accuracy of PPV predictions for subsequent blasts.
sections.applicability: Applies during construction-phase blasting operations requiring vibration monitoring and documentation of blast parameters.

sections.title: GROUNDWATER CONTROL
sections.summary: Overview of groundwater control for excavations below the water table, covering seepage control methods, cutoff wall types, and dewatering systems. Introduces the key approaches — sumps, wellpoints, deep wells, and various cutoff walls — and references applicable design procedures in DM 7.1 and other references.
key_points: Excavations below the groundwater table require control of seepage into the excavation and excess pore water pressures below the excavation bottom.
Primary dewatering methods include sumps, wellpoints, and deep wells; applicable limits vary with soil gradation (see Figure 2-21).
Slurry cutoff walls, concrete diaphragm walls, secant pile walls, and deep soil mix walls are most effective for reducing seepage.
Sheet piling is often considered impervious but seepage occurs through interlocks; interlock failure from hard driving can greatly increase seepage.
Design procedures for seepage analysis and dewatering are covered in Chapter 6 of DM 7.1.
sections.applicability: Applies whenever an excavation extends below the groundwater table and groundwater control measures must be selected and designed.

sections.title: Preliminary Considerations
sections.summary: Introduces the two primary groundwater control objectives for below-water-table excavations: controlling seepage into the excavation and controlling excess pore water pressures below the excavation bottom. Describes the most common dewatering methods (sumps, wellpoints, deep wells) and cutoff wall types, noting their relative effectiveness and limitations such as sheet pile interlock leakage.
sections.body:
Excavations below the groundwater table require groundwater control. This typically consists of controlling seepage into the excavation and controlling excess pore water pressures below the bottom of the excavation. Sumps, wellpoints, and deep wells are most commonly used to lower groundwater in excavations. Figure 2-21 illustrates applicable limits of these dewatering methods for different soil gradations.

Slurry cutoff walls (soil-bentonite or cement-soil-bentonite), concrete diaphragm walls, secant pile walls, and deep soil mix walls are the most effective walls for reducing seepage into an excavation. Concrete diaphragm walls may become part of the final structure. Sheet piling is often considered impervious but seepage occurs through the interlocks. If interlocks split due to hard driving, the rate of seepage can increase greatly. Special waterstops are available.
key_points: Two objectives: control seepage into the excavation and control excess pore water pressures below the excavation bottom.
Sumps, wellpoints, and deep wells are the most commonly used dewatering methods; selection depends on soil gradation.
Slurry cutoff walls, concrete diaphragm walls, secant pile walls, and deep soil mix walls are most effective at reducing seepage.
Sheet piling is not truly impervious — seepage occurs through interlocks, and interlock splitting from hard driving greatly increases leakage.
Concrete diaphragm walls can serve dual purpose as part of the permanent structure.
sections.applicability: Applies at the planning stage of any excavation that extends below the groundwater table, when selecting the type and combination of groundwater control measures.

sections.title: Permeability of Sheet Piling
sections.summary: Defines and explains the inverse specific resistance (ρ) of sheet pile walls per European Standard EN 12063, which characterizes interlock seepage. Provides Eq. 2-10 relating flow rate, unit weight of water, and differential pressure. Reports test data showing ρ ranges from ~10⁻³ cm/s (unsealed) to ~10⁻¹⁰ cm/s (sealed vinyl), and explains how ρ can be used to calculate flow rate through a sheet pile section.
sections.body:
The permeability of sheet pile walls, which occurs only through the interlocks, is usually expressed in terms of the inverse specific resistance, ρ, explained in European Standard EN 12063 (1999) which is defined as follows:

ρ = q / (γw · Δp)  (2-10)

where:
q = discharge or flow rate per unit height along the interlock,
γw = unit weight of water, and
Δp = differential pressure.

Seepage can be reduced by maintaining tension in the interlocks and/or by sealing the joints. Test sections have been performed on sheet piling sealed with various bitumen and swelling fillers (Sellmeijer et al. 1995). These tests indicate that ρ ranges from about 10⁻³ cm/sec for unsealed joints to about 10⁻⁹ cm/sec for sealed joints without tension in the joint. Bitumen sealants are slightly less effective than swelling sealants. Tests on vinyl sheet piling indicate ρ ranging from 10⁻⁵ cm/sec for unsealed joints in tension to about 10⁻¹⁰ cm/sec for sealed joints.

If ρ is known or assumed, Equation 2-10 can be rearranged to calculate the flow rate per unit length of interlock. This allows the flow rate through a section of sheet piling to be calculated. An example problem for leakage through sheet piling is shown in Figure 2-22.
key_points: Sheet pile wall seepage is characterized by inverse specific resistance ρ = q / (γw · Δp), per EN 12063.
For steel sheet piling: ρ ≈ 10⁻³ cm/s (unsealed) to 10⁻⁹ cm/s (sealed, no tension).
For vinyl sheet piling: ρ ≈ 10⁻⁵ cm/s (unsealed, in tension) to 10⁻¹⁰ cm/s (sealed).
Swelling sealants are slightly more effective than bitumen sealants at reducing interlock leakage.
Rearranging Eq. 2-10 allows calculation of flow rate per unit length of interlock when ρ is known.

equations.description: Inverse specific resistance of sheet pile interlock: ρ = q / (γw · Δp), where q is discharge per unit height, γw is unit weight of water, and Δp is differential pressure.

sections.applicability: Applies when evaluating or calculating seepage through sheet pile walls, particularly when selecting sealant type or estimating flow rates into an excavation.

sections.title: Methods of Controlling Groundwater
sections.summary: Presents a comprehensive table (Table 2-11) of groundwater control methods covering dewatering techniques (sumps, wellpoints, deep wells, jet-eductor wells) and cutoff wall systems (sheet piling, slurry trench, concrete diaphragm, secant/tangent pile, mix-in-place, and ground freezing), listing suitable soils, uses, and key limitations for each. Also references figures showing wellpoint and deep well construction details.
sections.body:
Table 2-11 lists methods of controlling groundwater, their applicability, and limitations. The methods represent groundwater lowering techniques including sumps, wellpoints, deep wells, and jet-eductor wells. Cutoff walls include sheet piling, slurry walls, concrete diaphragm walls, secant pile walls, and mix-in-place walls.

Figure 2-23 shows details of a wellpoint system and a deep well with a submersible pump. Figure 2-24 illustrates an example of a two stage well point system and a dewatering system using deep wells.

Design procedures related to seepage analysis and dewatering control are included in Chapter 6 of DM 7.1. Other good references include Mansur and Kaufman (1961) and Cedergren (1997).
key_points: Wellpoint systems with suction pumps are limited to ~18 ft lift; multi-stage systems at 15 ft vertical intervals are needed for greater depths.
Deep wells with submersible pumps and jet-eductor wells have no depth-of-drawdown limitation; deep wells can be sited clear of the excavation.
Cutoff walls (slurry trench, concrete diaphragm, secant/tangent pile, mix-in-place) generally need to be keyed into a less permeable stratum to reduce seepage.
Tangent pile walls leak more than secant pile walls because the piles do not overlap.
Ground freezing (ammonia/brine or liquid nitrogen) works in all saturated soils and rock; liquid nitrogen is faster but more expensive and causes some ground heave.
Properly sealed sheet pile interlocks can be as effective as slurry trench, concrete diaphragm, secant pile, and deep soil mix walls.
DM 7.1 Chapter 6 is the primary design reference for seepage analysis and dewatering control.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting and designing a groundwater control system for a construction excavation, requiring comparison of dewatering and cutoff methods against site soil conditions, depth, and space constraints.

sections.title: Problem Soils and Excavations
sections.summary: Introduces the topic of problem soil conditions affecting foundation and earth structure design, directing the reader to Chapter 1 for a general summary and to Tables 2-12 and 2-13 for specific design considerations for excavations in problem soils such as fissured clays, loess, sensitive clays, residual soils, talus, loose sands, and rock with weak planes.
sections.body: Chapter 1 provides a summary of many types of problem soil conditions that can affect the design of foundations and earth structures. Table 2-12 and Table 2-13 summarize important conditions for the design of excavations in problem soils.
key_points: Chapter 1 of the UFC provides a broader overview of problem soil types affecting foundations and earth structures.

Table 2-12 addresses sloped open cut excavations in problem soils, covering soil types including fissured stiff clays, desiccated clays, loess, sensitive clays, residual soils, talus, loose sands, and rock with weak planes.
Fissured stiff/highly plastic clays and soft shales may exhibit field shear resistance lower than lab tests; residual shear strength governs where prior failure surfaces exist.
Stiff desiccated highly plastic clays require use of fully softened drained strengths; desiccation cracks can extend up to 8 ft deep.
Loess slopes are more stable when cut near vertical to prevent infiltration; benches may be used for high slopes.
Sensitive clays can lose considerable strength upon remolding; a Liquidity Index > 1 (w > LL) indicates sensitivity.
Loose sands are susceptible to settlement under blast vibration, liquefaction under earthquake or static loading, and erosion/piping.
Rock with weak planes is susceptible to planar/wedge failures on discontinuities dipping toward the excavation and toppling of steeply dipping slabs.
tables: Table 2-12 Problem Soil Considerations for Sloped Open Cut Excavations
sections.applicability: Applies when designing excavations or foundations in any of the identified problem soil types, including fissured clays, collapsible soils, sensitive clays, residual soils, talus, loose sands, or rock with weak planes.

sections.title: NOTATION
sections.summary: Defines all variables and symbols used in Chapter 2 of UFC 3-220-20 covering deep, supported excavations. Includes geometric parameters (B, D, H), soil properties (su, K0, KA), wall performance metrics (Kwall, FBH), blasting variables (PPV, SD, W), and movement/distortion terms (δH, β). Essential reference for interpreting equations and design procedures throughout the chapter.
sections.body:
Variable | Definition
B | Excavation or trench width
B1 | Width of zone adjacent to excavation in clay that contributes to basal instability
Bs | Width of surcharge adjacent to excavation
D | Embedded depth of wall below base of excavation

key_points: B, D, and H define the primary geometry of the excavation: width, embedded wall depth, and excavation depth, respectively.
FBH (factor of safety against basal heave) and Hcrit (critical excavation depth in clay) are key stability metrics for clay soils.
su variants (su, su,b, su,d, su,h) distinguish undrained shear strength at different locations relative to the excavation base and wall.
Kwall (normalized wall stiffness) and K0/KA (earth pressure coefficients) govern lateral earth pressure and wall deformation calculations.
Blasting variables K (confinement factor), SD (scaled distance), W (charge weight), and PPV (peak particle velocity) support vibration and blast impact assessments.
β (angular distortion) and db (point separation distance) are used together for assessing differential movement and structural distortion.
α (adhesion factor) quantifies fine-grained soil–wall interface friction, relevant to passive resistance and wall design.

sections.title: SUGGESTED READING
sections.summary: A curated reference list for Chapter 2 topics, organized by subject area: Excavation Safety and Shoring (OSHA CFR Part 1926 Subpart P), Deep Excavations (FHWA NHI-07-071 and Clough & O'Rourke 1990), Dry Docks and Groundwater Control (Mazurkiewicz 1980 and USACE TM 5/818-5), and Dewatering (Mansur & Kaufman 1961; Cedergren 1997). Also includes a notation table of chapter variables and definitions.
sections.body:
Variable definitions referenced in this chapter:

∆p – Differential water pressure between the excavation and retained soil for sheet pile seepage
δV, δVi, δVm – Vertical movement of the ground adjacent to an excavation; m indicates maximum
εb – Horizontal strain of a structure caused by differential movement
γ, γt – Moist or total unit weight
γw – Unit weight of water
φʹ – Drained or effective stress friction angle
ρ – Specific resistance of sheet pile interlocks to seepage
σʹh – Effective horizontal stress

SUGGESTED READING:

Excavation Safety and Shoring:
Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA). 2020. CFR Part 1926, Subpart P, Excavations, with Appendices A - F. https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1926/1926SubpartP.

Deep Excavations:
FHWA. 2008. Earth Retaining Structures, FHWA NHI-07-071. U.S. Department of Transportation, Federal Highway Administration, Washington, DC.
Clough, G. W., and O'Rourke, T. D. 1990. "Construction Induced Movements of In situ Walls." Proc. of Conf. on Design and Performance of Earth Retaining Structures. ASCE Geotechnical Special Publication No. 25.

Dry Docks and Groundwater Control:
Mazurkiewicz, B.K. 1980. Design and Construction of Dry Docks. Trans Tech Publications, Rockport, MA.
USACE. 1983. Dewatering and Groundwater Control, TM 5/818-5/AFM 88-5. Department of the Army, Washington, DC.

Dewatering:
Mansur, C. and Kaufman, R. 1961. "Dewatering." Foundation Engineering, Ed. Leonards, McGraw Hill, 514 pp.
Cedergren, H. 1997. Seepage, Drainage, and Flow Nets, 3rd Ed., Wiley-Interscience, 496 pp.
key_points: OSHA CFR Part 1926 Subpart P is the primary regulatory reference for excavation safety and shoring requirements.
FHWA NHI-07-071 (2008) is the key design manual for deep earth retaining structures.
Clough & O'Rourke (1990) is the foundational reference for predicting construction-induced movements of in-situ walls.
Mazurkiewicz (1980) and USACE TM 5/818-5 cover dry dock design and groundwater control, respectively.
Mansur & Kaufman (1961) and Cedergren (1997) are classic dewatering and seepage references applicable to excavation drainage design.
